title: Rebuild a Tree From a Dashed Outline
statement:
A binary tree was written out in preorder (node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree). Each node was written as d dashes followed by its value, where d is the node's depth; the root has depth 0. Everything was glued together into one string outline, like "1-2--3-4".

If a node has only one child, that child is always the left child. Rebuild the tree and return it, written in level order with null for missing children.

examples.why: 2 and 4 have depth 1, so both are children of 1. 3 has depth 2 and comes right after 2, so it is 2's left child.
Each node has one child, and a single child always goes on the left, so the tree is a left-leaning chain.
After 8 the depth drops back to 1: 9 is the right child of 5, not a child of 8. Values have several digits, so read whole numbers.

constraints: The outline describes a valid tree
hints: First split the string into (depth, value) pairs: count dashes, then read digits until the next dash.
In preorder, the parent of a node at depth d is the most recent node seen at depth d − 1. How do you keep the most recent node at every depth?

Keep a stack holding the current root-to-node path. For a node at depth d, pop until the stack has exactly d nodes; the top is its parent. Attach it as left child if that slot is empty, otherwise as right child, then push it.

explain.intuition:
Preorder writes a node, then dives into its subtrees. So at any moment, the nodes "still open" are exactly the path from the root down to the last node written, and that path has one node per depth. When a node at depth d shows up, its parent must be the node at depth d − 1 on that path.

A stack holds the path. Pop until its length is d: everything deeper is finished, because preorder never returns to a closed subtree. The top is the parent. The first child a node receives goes left (preorder visits left first, and single children are left by the rule), the second goes right.
steps: Scan the string with an index. Count dashes to get depth, then read the digits into value.
Create the node. While the stack holds more than depth nodes, pop.
If the stack is not empty, attach the node to the top: as left if that is empty, otherwise as right.
At the end the bottom of the stack is the root; return it.
pitfalls: Reading values as single characters. "1-23" has the child 23, not 2 and 3.
Attaching a lone child on the right when the parent's left subtree is empty. The rule says single children are left.
Returning the top of the stack instead of the bottom. After the scan the top is the last node, not the root.

complexity.time: O(L) for an outline of length L
complexity.space: O(h) for the stack, plus the tree

solutions.title: Tokenize, then recurse by depth
solutions.idea: Turn the string into (depth, value) tokens. build(d) takes the next token if its depth is d, then builds the left and right subtrees at depth d + 1.

solutions.title: Stack of the current path
solutions.idea: The stack holds the path from the root to the last node. Pop down to the new node's depth, attach it to the top, push it.

followups: Write the reverse: turn a tree into this dashed outline.
Drop the "single child is left" rule and mark a missing left child with a special token instead. How does the parser change?
